---
title: "Git for group work"
---

## What this is for

Your group project lives in files: R scripts, a Quarto report, maybe some data.
Several of you will edit those files over several weeks. You need a way to do
that without emailing zip files, without `analysis_final_v3_ULO_REALLY_FINAL.R`,
and without silently overwriting each other's work.

That is what git and GitHub are for. By the end of this tutorial your group
will have:

- one GitHub repository that everybody can read and write
- a history of who changed what, when, and **why**
- a way to work at the same time without destroying each other's work
- a `main` branch that always runs

## The deal about AI doing the work

You will not memorise git commands. Claude Code will type them for you, and it
is better at writing commit messages than you are.

But you do have to understand **four ideas**, because when things go wrong —
and they will — the AI can fix the mechanics while only you can decide what is
*correct*. When two of you have written different interpretations of the same
result, no amount of AI can tell you which sentence your group means to publish.

::: {.callout-important}
## The bar you have to clear

By the end of [Part 1](01-concepts.qmd) you must be able to draw the four-places diagram
from memory and explain what a merge conflict is. That is the whole theory
requirement. Everything else you can delegate.
:::

## What you will build

A small R project called `penguin-clinic`: simulated clinic data, three
analysis scripts, and a shared Quarto report. It is deliberately structured so
that each group member owns one file — and so that one section of the report
is shared, to make you deal with a merge conflict on purpose, in a safe place,
before it happens for real at 23:00 the night before a deadline.

A worked version of the finished repository, with all its history and its pull
request, is here:
[github.com/ymaivali/penguin-clinic](https://github.com/ymaivali/penguin-clinic).

## How to read the code blocks

Most steps are shown twice:

::: {.callout-tip}
## Say this to Claude Code
> Commit my changes with a message explaining that I added the sex-stratified table.
:::

```bash
# what it actually runs
git add R/02-describe.R
git commit -m "Add sex-stratified descriptives"
```

Read the prompt. Glance at the commands. Do not memorise the commands.
